boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Petersburg (June 9) record (June 9, 1864) in the Richmond-Petersburg Campaign [June 1864-March 1865]. The assault record (VA063) begins on June 15; the frozen description's June 14-17 crossing of the James is later context. Army-wide returns, raid-wide and multi-action loss totals, and the siege as a whole are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.value: The frozen force text reads 7,000 (US 4,500; CS 2,500), the Union row carrying 4,500 as bounds and the Confederate row '2,500' as text only; the live field matches. Humphreys gives Gillmore 1,800 infantry of his own under Hawley and 1,200 of Hinks's, Kautz about 1,500 cavalry, and Wise's brigade, 2,400 strong, with such local troops as could be gathered defending Petersburg.
claims.rationale: Humphreys' Union components total about 4,500 and match the frozen Union figure; his Confederate figure covers Wise's brigade without the militia and Dearing's cavalry, which also appear in his account. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Humphreys says Gillmore, with Hinks and Hawley concurring, decided not to attempt the works and withdrew at half-past one, while Kautz attacked alone and was checked when Dearing's brigade, sent by Beauregard, came up. Gillmore says he held both positions expecting to hear from Kautz. Butler's indorsement, relayed by his chief of staff, called the affair disgraceful; Gillmore called the charge unmerited and unjust. The frozen commanders are Major General Gillmore (US) and General Beauregard (CS); the live page gives both as Brigadier General.
claims.rationale: Direction and blame are attributed as stated; Butler's and Gillmore's accounts are adversarial. The live ranks are not adopted. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

open_questions: Butler's June 9-14 papers (No. 1, heavily garbled; read, not selected), Hinks's, Kautz's and the other Union reports (Nos. 3-17), Wise's congratulatory orders and Colston's report (Nos. 18-19) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. Humphreys' The Virginia Campaign of ’64 and ’65 (1883) is an interested history by the Army of the Potomac's chief of staff, later commander of its Second Corps, in the same author family as the registered From Gettysburg to the Rapidan; it relies on Meade's, Hancock's, Warren's, Burnside's, Parke's and Wilson's reports and quotes Lee's, Beauregard's and Gordon's despatches, so it is not independent of those families. Gillmore's, Meade's, Hancock's, Burnside's, Wilson's, Hampton's, Stannard's and Lee's papers, printed in Official Records Series I, Volumes XXXVI (Part 2), XL, XLII and XLVI (Part 1), are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; each volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Lee's telegrams largely relay subordinates' reports. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
